stem.text: The diagram shows the effect of the introduction of a national minimum wage, W<sub>M</sub>, in an occupation where workers are employed by a profit-maximising monopsonist.

stem.alt: A monopsony labour market diagram with wage rate on the vertical axis and employment on the horizontal axis. An upward-sloping supply of labour curve S_L and a steeper upward-sloping marginal cost of labour curve MC_L both start from the origin; a downward-sloping demand/marginal revenue product curve MRP_L=D_L runs across the diagram. Before the minimum wage, the monopsonist employs at the quantity where MC_L crosses MRP_L=D_L (the smallest of three marked quantities, Q1), paying the wage W1 read off the supply curve at that quantity, point X. A horizontal minimum wage line at WM (above W1) is introduced. Three further points are marked: Y, directly above X on the WM line at quantity Q1 continued vertically; Z above Y, where MC_L crosses the WM line, at quantity Q3; and U, slightly right of Y, where the MRP_L=D_L curve crosses the WM line, at quantity Q3 (the new equilibrium employment level with the minimum wage). A fourth point V, at the highest marked wage W2, is where S_L crosses MRP_L=D_L at the largest quantity Q2 (the competitive equilibrium that would prevail without monopsony power).

stem.text: What happened to the total wages received by the workers in the occupation?

items: A  They decreased from OW<sub>2</sub>VQ<sub>2</sub> to OW<sub>M</sub>UQ<sub>3</sub>.
B  They decreased from OW<sub>2</sub>ZQ<sub>1</sub> to OW<sub>M</sub>UQ<sub>3</sub>.
C  They increased from OW<sub>1</sub>XQ<sub>1</sub> to OW<sub>M</sub>YQ<sub>1</sub>.
D  They increased from OW<sub>1</sub>XQ<sub>1</sub> to OW<sub>M</sub>UQ<sub>3</sub>.

explanation.text: Without the minimum wage, a profit-maximising monopsonist employs where MC_L = MRP_L (quantity Q1), then pays the lowest wage that attracts that many workers by reading off the labour supply curve S_L — wage W1, giving total wages OW1XQ1 (wage × quantity). A minimum wage set between W1 and the competitive wage W2 flattens the monopsonist's effective marginal cost curve at WM up to the point where it meets S_L again; the firm then re-optimises where this new MC_L curve meets MRP_L=D_L, at the larger quantity Q3 and the higher wage WM, giving the new total wages OW<sub>M</sub>UQ3 — both the wage and the quantity employed have risen, so total wages must have increased.

optionAnalysis.text: OW2VQ2 is the fully competitive outcome (where S_L meets MRP_L at quantity Q2), not the original monopsony outcome before the minimum wage was introduced.
OW2ZQ1 mismatches the wage W2 (the competitive wage) with the monopsony quantity Q1 and point Z, which is not a valid total-wages rectangle for either the before or after situation.
OWMYQ1 uses the new minimum wage but the old (smaller) quantity Q1, which is not the correct post-minimum-wage employment level — employment rises to Q3, not Q1, once the minimum wage is introduced.

The before situation is correctly OW1XQ1 (wage W1, quantity Q1) and the after situation is OW<sub>M</sub>UQ3 (wage WM, quantity Q3) — both wage and quantity rose, so total wages (the area of each rectangle) increased.

reasoningChain: Identify the original monopsony equilibrium: MC_L = MRP_L at quantity Q1, wage W1 read off the supply curve — total wages = W1 × Q1 = area OW1XQ1.

Identify the new equilibrium after the minimum wage WM (set between W1 and the competitive wage W2) flattens the effective MC_L curve: the firm now employs where this new curve meets MRP_L, at the larger quantity Q3, paying wage WM — total wages = WM × Q3 = area OWMUQ3.
Compare the two rectangles: since both wage and quantity increased, total wages must have increased, not decreased.

inferredMistakes.text: Assuming a minimum wage always reduces employment (as in a competitive labour market), without recognising that in a monopsony, a minimum wage set appropriately can increase both the wage and the quantity of labour employed.

bullets: Option C was a common incorrect answer.
This suggests some candidates did not appreciate that the higher wage would lead to an increase from Q<sub>1</sub> to Q<sub>3</sub> in the number of workers employed.
